analysis.one_liner: Strips federal regulators of LNG terminal permitting and gas trade oversight, handing those decisions to states.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by one representative with no cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would remove the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's power to approve or block liquefied natural gas (LNG) terminals and would end federal oversight of companies that import or export natural gas. Siting decisions would shift to the states and local communities, and federal agencies working on LNG safety, environmental, or security questions would have to consult the host state and post their documents publicly. It never moved past its first committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: States and communities hosting or considering LNG terminals would gain real authority over whether a terminal gets built, plus guaranteed public access to safety and environmental documents — unless the Homeland Security Department deems them security-sensitive. Gas trading companies would gain by having federal import/export oversight repealed.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals FERC's authority to approve or deny the siting, construction, expansion, or operation of LNG terminals, shifting that decision away from a federal commission [S2] [S3].
Removes federal preemption over state and local safety concerns for LNG terminals by striking the relevant oversight provisions of the Natural Gas Act [S2] [S3].
Requires any FERC agreements or activities on the environmental impact, public safety, or security of an LNG facility to include input from and consultation with the host state [S2] [S3].

Requires the reports and documents from those FERC activities to be made available to the public in print and online, unless the Secretary of Homeland Security determines they are vital to national security [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: LNG terminal developers and companies importing or exporting natural gas would bear new uncertainty: states could veto terminals FERC once approved, and a patchwork of state rules would replace one federal process. The federal government would also lose a uniform safety and siting framework.
analysis.who_pays_short: LNG terminal developers and gas traders

drawbacks.text: Repealing FERC's federal safety oversight over LNG terminal construction means safety standards near these hazardous facilities would depend entirely on state and local capacity, which varies widely [S2] [S3].

Ending federal regulatory oversight of natural gas importers and exporters removes a layer of federal review of foreign gas commerce, an honest cost an energy-security-minded supporter would have to acknowledge [S2].

Replacing one federal permitting process with state-by-state control could make LNG terminal development slower and less predictable, which industry critics of the bill would argue raises energy costs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives host communities genuine leverage over large, hazardous industrial facilities in their backyards and mandates public transparency, which is a real benefit. The cost is that federal expertise and uniform safety oversight for LNG terminals is repealed rather than supplemented, and the gas trade side of the bill is straight deregulation with no replacement protections. A better version might have added local authority without deleting the federal safety layer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and no further action was ever taken on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. David Wu introduced the Local Control for Energy and Environment Act on September 14, 2010 [S1] [S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on the day of introduction, and the record shows no markup, hearing, or floor action afterward [S5].
The 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, so the bill expired without a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held. LNG terminal developers and gas import/export companies kept the single federal permitting process FERC administers instead of facing state veto power, and federal authority over LNG siting and gas trade went unchanged. Communities near proposed terminals gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. David Wu
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to shift LNG terminal siting authority from FERC to states and require public disclosure of safety documents; it drew no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever held, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, and no vote was ever taken, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: LNG terminal developers and natural gas importers/exporters
industries.note: The bill repeals federal oversight of natural gas import and export commerce, a straight gain for gas trading companies. But it also strips FERC's exclusive federal permitting power over terminals and lets states block projects, so a developer's fate would depend on the host state rather than a federal review it knows how to navigate.

industries.industry: States and local governments near LNG facilities
industries.note: Host states would gain mandatory consultation on LNG safety, environmental, and security matters and an effective veto over terminal siting, power currently preempted by federal law.
